hints: Focus on what conductivity and malleability tell you about bonding, since both forms have very high boiling points.
Notice grey tin is brittle, has a huge boiling point but conducts nothing in solid or liquid, which matches a giant covalent lattice like diamond or silicon.
Consider why white tin conducting well as a solid and being malleable points to delocalised electrons, then link the two structures together.
walkthrough:
**Recall what each giant structure does**

Giant structures all have very high melting and boiling points because lots of strong bonds must be broken. The difference is in conductivity and malleability.

Rule to use:
$$\text{metallic conducts as solid and liquid, covalent conducts as neither, ionic conducts as liquid only}$$

**Identify grey tin**

Grey tin has a boiling point over 2500 K, so it is giant. It does not conduct in solid or liquid and it is brittle.

That fits giant covalent perfectly. There are no free electrons or ions to carry charge, and the rigid directional covalent bonds shatter rather than bend.

**Identify white tin**

White tin also has a boiling point over 2500 K, so it is also giant. But it conducts well in both solid and liquid and it is malleable.

That is classic giant metallic behaviour. Delocalised electrons move in solid and liquid to conduct, and layers of cations can slide to allow malleability.

**Describe the change**

Going from grey to white is therefore a change from a giant covalent lattice with localised electrons to a giant metallic lattice with delocalised electrons.

options.A: Incorrect. A giant ionic lattice would conduct electricity when molten because ions become free to move. Grey tin does not conduct even as a liquid, and white tin conducts as a solid, which ionic lattices cannot do.
options.B: Correct. Grey tin shows giant covalent properties (very high boiling point, non-conductor in solid and liquid, brittle). White tin shows giant metallic properties (very high boiling point, good conductor in solid and liquid, malleable).
options.C: Incorrect and backwards. Grey tin cannot be giant ionic because it fails to conduct when liquid. Also tin is a single element, so it cannot form an ionic lattice which needs positive and negative ions from different elements.
options.D: Incorrect for the starting point. Grey tin is not ionic because an ionic solid would conduct when melted. Its lack of conductivity in both states plus brittleness and very high boiling point identifies it as giant covalent, not giant ionic.
